You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

mem = rlm.harness.create_memory(
 title='ARC task-d01637b5 verified line-extension and periodic border completion rule',
 content='''ARC task-d01637b5 VERIFIED RULE (solved after six wrong attempts; final correct grid followed this exact procedure): The input is a rectangular monochrome border B enclosing a small orthogonal ladder/striped object made of green 3 rails and red 2 rungs on 0 background. Remove the outer border and extend the internal pattern across the whole same-size grid.

For a HORIZONTAL object (the test orientation): the two 3 rows become full rows of 3 across the entire width. Every cell that is 2 in a rung row stays 2; all other cells in that row become 0. For each column containing 2, fill every ordinary/non-rung/non-3 row in that column with border color B. All remaining cells become 0. Thus the rung rows interrupt the vertical B lines with 0 and 2 values, while the 3 rows override everything with 3. VERTICAL objects are the exact transpose: 3 columns extend fully, rows containing 2 receive B outside the object/rungs, and 0/3/2 structure is preserved as demonstrated.

Crucial border/periodicity detail: do NOT blindly retain the old right or bottom border. Treat the 2-rung pattern as periodic through the border. A border column/row becomes B on ordinary rows only if that column/row is part of the periodic 2 band; otherwise it becomes 0. On a rung row it is 2 if the periodic band reaches it, otherwise 0. Example from verified 16x19 test: 2 cells at columns 1,4,7,10,13,16, so ordinary rows were [0,7,0,0,7,0,0,7,0,0,7,0,0,7,0,0,7,0,0]. The last column 18 was 0 (next period would be 19, outside), not 7. Rung row 6 was [0,2,0,0,2,0,0,2,0,0,2,0,0,2,0,0,2,0,0]. Rows 5 and 7 were all 3. Every other row matched the ordinary row. Demo with 2 bands reaching the last border instead yields B in ordinary rows and 2 in rung rows there.

Rejected errors: keeping the entire bottom border B; putting B throughout rung rows; retaining a non-periodic right border as B; rotating/transposing the orientation arbitrarily. Determine extension directly from the object orientation and periodic rung columns/rows.''',
 path='arc/task-d01637b5', global_=True)
print(mem.id)
await refine.run(instructions='Persist the verified task-d01637b5 rule globally, emphasizing periodic completion at borders and the exact successful horizontal construction.', global_=True)
